raw_condition_label: EA artifact usability design: cognitive fit, complexity restraint, and horizon-appropriate granularity
readiness_statement: EA artifacts function as usable decision-support tools for architecture-led transformation only when their information presentation format matches the decision task (cognitive fit), their complexity is restrained to a small number of comprehensible elements (information processing limits), and their level of detail is matched to their planning horizon and organizational scope (uncertainty principle) -- attempting wide-scope, long-horizon, high-detail artifacts simultaneously is not achievable.
mechanism: Presentation formats that match the mental representation of the task at hand (e.g., graphical landscape diagrams for spatial integration tasks, tabular inventories for symbolic lookup tasks) improve problem-solving performance; human short-term memory can process only about 5-9 chunks of information at once, so artifacts must be hierarchically structured or split by audience to remain usable; and because business environments are inherently uncertain, artifacts covering wider scopes and longer horizons must sacrifice detail, while narrower/shorter-horizon artifacts can be more detailed.
operationalization_hint: Assess whether EA artifact presentation formats are matched to their intended decision tasks, whether artifacts are structured into a limited number of hierarchical categories (roughly five to ten items per level) rather than exhaustive detail, and whether the level of granularity in each artifact type is proportionate to its planning horizon and scope.

raw_condition_label: gap between prescribed EA frameworks and actual successful EA practice as a caveat condition
readiness_statement: Formal, comprehensive EA frameworks and methodologies (e.g., Zachman, TOGAF, DoDAF, FEAF) prescribing linear step-wise processes, exhaustive artifact taxonomies, and detailed future-state documentation are not followed by successful EA practices in organizations, even when their use is formally declared; treating adherence to such frameworks as a readiness condition is therefore a caveat that can mislead transformation assessments.
mechanism: EA frameworks originate largely from fashion-setting networks (major consultancies, gurus, industry consortia) whose promotional influence creates a transitory collective belief in their effectiveness under conditions of high uncertainty, independent of rigorous empirical validation; documented cases (e.g., DoDAF costing up to $400 million, FEAF up to $1 billion in the US federal government with limited use) show these frameworks are frequently adopted purely declaratively or abandoned, while actually-successful practices rely on pragmatic, non-standard artifact collections instead.
operationalization_hint: When assessing an organization's EA/transformation readiness, distinguish formal declared adoption of an EA framework from evidence of framework-independent, pragmatic artifact usage (boundary-object-quality artifacts, collaborative stakeholder development) actually observed in the organization's real planning and decision processes.
page_or_section: Contrast theories / Management fashion theory, pp. 292-294
rationale: The critical review concludes that successful EA practices do not resemble prescribed linear, exhaustive frameworks and explains this mismatch through management-fashion theory. The CF accurately flags declared framework adoption as insufficient evidence of effective EA practice.

raw_condition_label: digital seizing capability / strategic agility
readiness_statement: Building on Teece's foundational theory, seizing a sensed opportunity requires astutely designing or redesigning a business model to capture value, committing resources under uncertainty despite biases that favor the status quo, and overcoming established decision rules (e.g., capital-budgeting processes biased toward predictable cash flows) that can starve new initiatives of investment.
mechanism: Business models articulate the value proposition, technology and feature choices, target segments, and value-capture mechanism, and must be crafted astutely because technological innovation alone does not guarantee commercial success; investment decisions are undermined by well-documented biases -- the isolation effect and certainty effect that produce excessive risk aversion, anti-cannibalization bias, and program-persistence bias from bureaucratic committee-based approval processes -- so seizing capability also requires organizational disciplines (decentralizing decision rights, reducing management layers, seeking outside views, using unbiased economic-depreciation data) that counteract these biases and allow committed, timely investment.
operationalization_hint: Assess whether the organization has an explicit, deliberately designed (not just inherited) business model for the transformation initiative, whether investment decision processes show signs of program-persistence or anti-cannibalization bias, and whether corrective mechanisms (reduced approval layers, outside-view reviews, economic rather than purely accounting-based depreciation analysis) are in place.
rationale: Teece's account of seizing emphasizes deliberate business-model design, resource commitment under uncertainty, and countering decision biases. The CF accurately operationalizes these conditions for transformation investment choices.

mechanism: Committee-based, multilevel approval processes that are useful for control purposes also slow decision making and reinforce the status quo, generating a program-persistence bias that starves new initiatives; established assets intensify the isolation effect (evaluating options one at a time rather than as a portfolio) and the certainty effect (discounting probable gains relative to certain ones), producing excessive risk aversion specifically in incumbents; incumbents may also confuse accounting depreciation with real economic depreciation and thereby avoid profit-enhancing cannibalization of their own products.

mechanism: Because EA models are built from structural and architectural elements (processes, capabilities, systems, organizational units), they cannot directly represent culture, informal power dynamics, or company politics; as a result, the same business model can lead to different actual business organizations depending on non-architectural, philosophical, or political choices, and detailed organizational design ends up being shaped as much or more by company politics as by the formally modeled business model or strategy.

raw_condition_label: critical success factors for durable IT governance design (transparency, active design, education, simplicity, exception handling, multi-level governance, aligned incentives, infrequent redesign)
readiness_statement: Effective, durable IT governance requires deliberately designing for eight critical success factors: transparency of decisions to all managers, active (rather than ad hoc, silo-by-silo) design of governance mechanisms, infrequent redesign (reserved for major strategy shifts, not routine economic fluctuations), ongoing manager education about governance, simplicity (targeting a small number of performance goals), a clearly stated exception-handling process, governance designed coherently across multiple organizational levels (enterprise, division, business unit), and alignment between incentive and reward systems and the behaviors governance is meant to encourage.
mechanism: Each factor addresses a specific failure mode: covertly-made decisions erode confidence and rule-following (transparency); reactive, silo-by-silo governance mechanisms limit strategic impact (active design); frequent redesign signals the structure was poorly designed and prevents the organization from learning to use it (infrequent redesign); uneducated managers cannot be held accountable and re-litigate settled decisions (education); too many simultaneous goals create conflicting desirable behaviors (simplicity); unsanctioned workarounds proliferate without an open, escalating exception process that still enables learning (exception handling); disconnected governance at different organizational levels creates pressure points (multi-level design); and misaligned incentives undermine governance regardless of how well it is otherwise designed (aligned incentives).
operationalization_hint: Audit the organization's IT governance design against each of the eight factors: is it visible to all managers; was it actively and coherently designed rather than accreted ad hoc; has it avoided being redesigned in response to routine (non-strategic) events; is there an ongoing governance education program; does it target a small number of clear goals; is there a documented, escalating exception process (e.g., a one-page dual business/technical justification, as at UPS); is governance explicitly connected across enterprise, division, and business-unit levels; and are incentive and reward systems aligned with the behaviors governance is meant to produce.

rationale: The governance study specifies eight critical success factors and explains their practical role in durable governance design. The CF accurately turns the authors' factors into an audit checklist.

readiness_statement: Achieving business-IT alignment requires selecting one of four cross-domain alignment perspectives -- strategy execution (business strategy drives organizational and IS infrastructure design), technology transformation (business strategy drives IT strategy and IS infrastructure without being constrained by current organization design), competitive potential (IT strategy shapes and enables new business strategy), and service level (IT strategy drives world-class internal IS service delivery) -- and then assigning top-management and IS-management roles and performance criteria that fit that specific perspective, since a role or metric appropriate to one perspective (e.g., IS-as-cost-center under strategy execution) will misfit and undermine alignment under another (e.g., IS-as-technology-architect under technology transformation).
mechanism: Each alignment perspective implies a different locus of strategic driver and therefore a different appropriate role split: under strategy execution, top management is the strategy formulator and IS management is the strategy implementor assessed as a cost or service center; under technology transformation, top management is the technology visionary and IS management is the technology architect assessed on technology leadership; under competitive potential, top management is the business visionary and IS management is the catalyst assessed on business leadership; and under service level, top management is the prioritizer and IS management is executive leadership assessed on customer satisfaction -- applying the wrong role and criteria combination for the perspective actually in play is a source of alignment failure even when the four-domain model itself is understood.
operationalization_hint: Identify which of the four alignment perspectives currently describes the organization's dominant transformation logic (which domain is acting as the driver), and check whether top-management and IS-management roles and performance-assessment criteria have been explicitly matched to that perspective rather than defaulting to the traditional strategy-execution role split (business strategist plus IS cost-center implementor) regardless of context.

raw_condition_label: value creation and capture through information, multisided business models, and control of digital industry architecture
readiness_statement: Digital business strategy requires deliberately identifying and pursuing new sources of value creation and capture specific to digital contexts: monetizing information itself (beyond its use as an input to physical products or services), designing multisided or multilayered business models that give away value in one layer to capture it in another, coordinating value capture across complex networks of interdependent partners, and appropriating disproportionate value by controlling key points in the digital industry architecture.
mechanism: Digital conditions make it possible to build entire business models around curating, personalizing, and monetizing information (rather than only using it to support physical products or services), and around multisided platforms where a firm gives away one product or service layer (e.g., Android) to capture value at a different layer (e.g., advertising); because digital ecosystems (e.g., mobile) require coordination across multiple interdependent players (app developers, OS providers, hardware makers, carriers), value capture depends on holding strategically valuable control points in that network -- as illustrated by Apple capturing a disproportionate profit share in mobile despite a smaller market share, by controlling the industry architecture around its own product and revenue-sharing position.
operationalization_hint: Assess whether the organization's digital strategy explicitly identifies which layer or layers of a potential multisided business model it intends to monetize (versus giving away), whether it has mapped the network of interdependent partners required for its digital offering and identified which control points would let it appropriate a disproportionate share of network value, and whether information itself (not just physical products or services) is treated as a distinct source of monetizable value.

rationale: The source directly discusses information-based value, multilayered multisided models, coordinated ecosystem value capture, and architectural control points.

raw_condition_label: relational mechanisms matter most in early-stage IT governance, structures are easier to implement than processes
readiness_statement: The relative importance of IT governance structures, processes, and relational mechanisms shifts with an organization's IT governance maturity stage: structures (e.g., steering committees) are generally easier to establish than processes (e.g., portfolio management), and relational mechanisms (e.g., informal meetings, cross-training, knowledge sharing) matter most while governance is still being initiated, becoming less critical once structures and processes are already embedded in day-to-day culture at mature organizations.
mechanism: In this study's highly aligned organizations, which had been building IT governance for more than five years, structures and processes were already embedded in daily practice and organizational culture, reducing the marginal need to actively manage relational aspects; by contrast, the poorly aligned organizations were still in an early, start-up phase of IT governance where motivating people and creating awareness (relational mechanisms) were relatively more important -- meaning relational-mechanism maturity alone did not clearly differentiate high from low performers in this cross-sectional comparison, even though the literature stresses their general importance.
operationalization_hint: When assessing IT governance readiness for transformation, account for the organization's governance maturity stage: expect relational mechanisms (informal meetings, cross-training, knowledge management, visible leadership modeling) to matter most during early governance rollout, and expect the relative payoff from further investment in structures and processes (versus relational mechanisms) to change as governance becomes embedded in the culture over multiple years.
rationale: The paper supports the maturity-stage contingency: processes are harder to implement than structures, while relational mechanisms were not clearly demonstrated overall and are described as likely important during initiation.

raw_condition_label: Delphi-validated perceived effectiveness and ease of implementation as a two-dimensional practice-prioritization condition
readiness_statement: Prioritizing which IT governance practices to implement first should account for two independent dimensions -- perceived effectiveness and perceived ease of implementation -- since some practices are both highly effective and easy to implement (e.g., IT steering committees, CIO reporting to the CEO/COO), while others are perceived as highly effective but comparatively hard to implement (e.g., benefits management and reporting, charge-back arrangements), and still others (e.g., COBIT, IT governance assurance and self-assessment) may be valuable at a higher level of abstraction without scoring highly on either dimension individually.
mechanism: A panel of 22 senior IT, business, and consulting experts rated all 33 candidate IT governance practices independently on a 0-5 scale for perceived effectiveness and perceived ease of implementation; because these two dimensions do not always move together, treating important practice as a single undifferentiated concept risks either underinvesting in high-effectiveness-but-harder practices or overinvesting effort in easy-but-lower-value practices; frameworks like COBIT, which operate at a higher level of abstraction, can still be valuable because many of the individually-rated effective detailed practices are integral parts of such frameworks even when the framework itself does not score as high individually.
operationalization_hint: When selecting which IT governance practices to roll out first, plot or rank candidate practices on both perceived effectiveness and perceived ease of implementation (via expert panel or similar structured elicitation) rather than a single combined priority score, and sequence early efforts toward practices that are both effective and easy, while planning longer-term efforts for high-effectiveness/low-ease practices such as benefits management and reporting or charge-back arrangements.

readiness_statement: Board-level IT governance mechanisms -- an IT strategy committee at the board of directors and dedicated IT expertise on the board -- are widely promoted in IT governance literature as essential given the board's prime responsibility for governance, but are rated by industry experts as comparatively low in both perceived effectiveness and perceived ease of implementation, and were not adopted by any of the extreme-case organizations studied except one with an atypical, closely-held ownership structure.
mechanism: Making a board of directors more IT-literate or establishing a dedicated board-level IT strategy committee is difficult to achieve in practice (reflected in a near-lowest ease-of-implementation score for board IT expertise), and in typical shareholder-governed organizations, board representatives are primarily concerned with core financial results rather than operational IT issues, making such structures both hard to implement and of limited perceived value in most contexts; the exception was a family-owned organization whose board (composed of family owners rather than external shareholders) operated much closer to daily operations.
operationalization_hint: Before treating board-level IT governance structures (board IT strategy committee, dedicated board IT expertise) as a necessary readiness condition, assess the organization's ownership and board-involvement model (e.g., closely-held or family-owned versus typical shareholder-governed), since these structures may be neither feasible nor high-value outside of atypical ownership contexts, despite their prominence in IT governance literature and standards (e.g., ITGI, COBIT).

raw_condition_label: change efficacy via cognitive appraisal of task demands, resource availability, and situational factors
readiness_statement: Transformation readiness requires a shared, favorable organizational appraisal of whether members know what implementation will take (task demands), whether adequate resources exist (resource availability), and whether the situation currently supports action (situational factors).
mechanism: Change efficacy is a collective judgment of implementation capability, analogous to Bandura's collective efficacy; it is not the same as possessing resources, but the shared belief that available resources and conditions are sufficient to execute the change.
operationalization_hint: Assess organizational members' shared confidence separately along the three appraisal dimensions (task demands, resources, situational factors) rather than as a single generic confidence score.

mechanism: Technology investment at the operational level only pays off if the executive level secures the policies/standards/infrastructure that let it be used properly, and the executive level in turn only functions if the strategic level has committed vision, resources, and change-management leadership -- meaning readiness gaps at any one level (e.g., strong technology adoption without policy/infrastructure support) undermine the digital transformation regardless of investment at other levels.
operationalization_hint: Assess an organization's DT readiness separately at the operational (technology-in-use), executive (policy/standards/infrastructure), and strategic (vision/resource-allocation/change-leadership) levels rather than treating "digital readiness" as a single undifferentiated construct.

raw_condition_label: temporal experience appraisal (TEA) model: prior digitalization sentiment shapes DT predispositions, which shape willingness to participate
readiness_statement: Employee-level transformation readiness follows a temporal causal chain -- past experience with digitalization shapes employee sentiment (stimulus), which shapes cognitive and emotional predispositions toward digital transformation (organism), which in turn determines employees' willingness to participate in DT initiatives (response) -- validated empirically (positive, significant path coefficients) in medium-to-large enterprises in both the US and Vietnam, with no significant cross-country difference.
mechanism: Because a DT initiative itself is too complex, novel, and ambiguous at the outset to function as a direct stimulus employees can evaluate, employees instead rely on their accumulated, fuzzy, gist-based appraisal of prior digitalization experiences as the reference point from which predispositions -- and ultimately willingness to participate -- are formed, even before a formal DT initiative is announced.
operationalization_hint: When assessing organizational transformation readiness, audit employees' sentiment toward *prior* digitalization efforts (not just attitudes toward the upcoming DT initiative itself), since this prior sentiment is the empirically-demonstrated leading indicator of future participation willingness.

raw_condition_label: early-stage employee participation as a uniquely high-leverage window for shaping transformation direction and reducing later resistance
readiness_statement: Employee participation in the initial stages of a DT initiative -- before new work practices become routinized -- is disproportionately consequential: early engagement lets employees shape the transformation's direction, fosters ownership that reduces later resistance, and allows organizations to proactively address emerging risks via bottom-up input, whereas after routinization, employees are reduced to executors of fixed procedures with severely restricted opportunity to influence or resist, making early non-participation predictive of sustained disengagement and blame-shifting if the initiative later fails.
mechanism: The dynamics of change are most fluid and open to influence during early phases; once routinized, changes become non-negotiable fixed procedures, which structurally forecloses the window during which participation could have prevented resistance -- meaning organizations that defer employee engagement until implementation or rollout have already lost the highest-leverage opportunity to secure buy-in.
operationalization_hint: Prioritize securing employee participation (planning input, feedback channels, cross-functional support roles) specifically during the pre-routinization early stage of a DT initiative, treating post-rollout participation efforts as a structurally weaker substitute.

title: A new proposed model to assess the digital organizational readiness to maximize the results of the digital transformation in SMEs
paper_authors: Silva, R.P.; Mamede, H.S.; Santos, V.
authors: Silva, R.P.; Mamede, H.S.; Santos, V.
raw_condition_label: formal distinction between readiness (behaviors) and maturity (implementation status) as a transformation-assessment condition
readiness_statement: Digital transformation assessment models conflate two distinct constructs that should be measured separately: maturity, which measures how far an organization has progressed in implementing something (e.g., how deployed a CRM platform is), and readiness, which measures whether the behaviors necessary to maximize the results of that implementation are present and consistently practiced (e.g., whether the organization actually uses the CRM to embed customer insights in decision-making) -- a review of 24 existing models found most fail to separate these constructs, defaulting readiness to "being finished" rather than "being ready to adopt change."
mechanism: Because maturity captures deployment status while readiness captures whether an organization has internalized the behaviors needed to extract value from that deployment, a technically mature implementation with low behavioral readiness will fail to generate expected returns -- explaining why organizations with similar technology adoption levels achieve divergent DT outcomes, and why over 70% of DT initiatives reportedly fail to reach expected value despite technology being in place.
operationalization_hint: When assessing an organization's DT status, score maturity (deployment/implementation progress) and readiness (behavioral consistency in leveraging what is deployed) as two separate, non-substitutable metrics rather than a single combined maturity score.
page_or_section: Section "Readiness as a set of behaviors", Table 1
canonical_label: Readiness as distinct construct from maturity
cluster_label: Readiness as distinct construct from maturity
rationale: The paper explicitly distinguishes readiness as behavior-oriented from maturity/deployment-oriented models and notes that prior models often blur the two concepts.

raw_condition_label: two-dimensional readiness-level scale (behavior frequency x behavior management consistency) with four qualitative levels
readiness_statement: Organizational readiness at the subcategory level should be scored along two independent dimensions -- how frequently a target behavior occurs and how consistently/deliberately it is managed (versus occurring accidentally) -- mapped onto a 1-10 Likert scale that aggregates into four qualitative levels: Immature (behavior absent/no action), Unstructured (behavior sometimes present, evolving), Structured (behavior often present, evolving toward advanced), and Advanced (behavior consistently present, measured, and continuously improved), with the transition from Unstructured to Structured representing the largest single step in the model.
mechanism: Separating frequency from management-consistency lets an assessment distinguish between a behavior that happens by chance (high frequency, low management -- e.g., ad hoc innovation) and one that is deliberately embedded (both dimensions high), which a single-axis maturity scale cannot distinguish; the model treats vertical progress (better management) and horizontal progress (higher frequency) as two independent improvement paths.
operationalization_hint: Score each of the 20 subcategories on both frequency and management-consistency axes separately, using the resulting four-level color-coded classification (red/orange/yellow/green) to identify whether a subcategory's gap is a frequency problem or a management-consistency problem.
page_or_section: Section "Readiness levels and measuring dimensions", Figs. 3-4
rationale: The DORAM proposal explicitly measures behavior frequency and management, distinguishes horizontal and vertical progress, and identifies the unstructured-to-structured transition as the largest step.

raw_condition_label: EA maturity level should determine which strategic-planning path an organization follows
readiness_statement: Organizations with no or nascent enterprise architecture (maturity level 0-1) should follow architecture-creation tasks when elaborating strategic actions during IS strategic planning, while organizations with an established architecture (maturity level 2-5) should instead follow architecture-implementation/maintenance tasks -- the appropriate planning process branches explicitly on the organization's assessed architecture maturity level rather than using one uniform planning sequence for all organizations.
mechanism: The tasks needed to progress differ fundamentally depending on whether an architecture must first be created versus already exists and needs implementation or upkeep; applying a maintenance-oriented process to an organization with no architecture (or vice versa) would misallocate effort.
operationalization_hint: Before applying an EA-driven strategic planning method, explicitly assess architecture maturity level first (per an EACMM-style 0-5 scale) and route the organization to the corresponding creation vs. implementation/maintenance task set rather than a single generic sequence.
rationale: The EAISSP method explicitly branches at maturity levels 0–1 versus 2–5, assigning architecture-creation tasks to the former and implementation or maintenance tasks to the latter. The CF accurately represents this method rule.

mechanism: Foundational technical capabilities (data quality, application quality, infrastructure, project management discipline) appear to function as a constant baseline requirement regardless of maturity stage, whereas strategic alignment, governance, security, and human-capital conditions become progressively more critical differentiators as an organization advances -- meaning readiness assessments should not apply flat importance weights to all enabling conditions across all maturity stages.
operationalization_hint: When assessing which enabling conditions to prioritize at a given maturity stage, treat technical/foundational conditions as necessary baseline investments at all stages, but weight strategic, governance, security, and human-capital conditions more heavily as the organization/initiative matures.
rationale: The ANOVA/Tukey results state that strategy and business importance rises with BI maturity while data, applications, network/infrastructure and project management remain equal. The CF accurately expresses the maturity-dependent prioritisation result.

raw_condition_label: cross-organizational data governance requires overcoming trust, coordination-cost, and skill barriers before data-sharing ecosystems can scale
readiness_statement: Beyond technical capability, data-sharing transformation initiatives (data spaces) require organizations to overcome reluctance to share proprietary data, demonstrate the business value of data sharing, secure sufficiently skilled IT personnel, and absorb the cross-organizational coordination costs of aligning data models, standards, and business processes across multiple autonomous actors.
mechanism: Data-sharing ecosystems involve multiple independent organizations that must reach consensus on both technical and organizational governance capabilities; this consensus-building is costly and slow because it requires balancing competitive concerns (fear of losing advantage by sharing know-how) against collective value creation, and requires a trusted, resourced coordinating body to reach agreement.
operationalization_hint: Before committing to a data-space/data-sharing initiative, verify: an explicit trust-building governance framework defining roles/responsibilities/decision rights; a demonstrated business case for data-sharing value; availability of skilled personnel; and a designated, resourced governing body with authority to enforce cross-organizational agreements.
rationale: The discussion identifies trust building, cross-organisational coordination costs, consensus on standards and processes, and the need for a resourced governance operator as data-space barriers. The CF accurately consolidates these literature-derived constraints.

readiness_statement: Enterprises undertaking architecture-led transformation must first establish strategic architecture (vision, target customer segments, product/service portfolio, human-capital strategy, and capacity objectives) before constructing enterprise architecture (business, data, application, technology domains); building EA before SA clarity results in technology investments disconnected from business needs (the "technology-driven trap") and resource waste.
mechanism: Strategic architecture functions as the organization's directional "brain," determining which EA domains and priorities matter (e.g., a venue positioned as a premier concert venue needs different EA priorities than one positioned as a community activity center), while EA feeds back "capability feedback" on technical feasibility and resource constraints, forming a bidirectional strategy-execution loop; skipping the SA step causes IT/system investments to be made without a clear business rationale.
operationalization_hint: Before committing to EA domain investments, verify that SA elements (customer segments, product/service scope, human-capital strategy, capacity/operations targets) are explicitly defined and stakeholder-validated; treat mismatched SA-EA sequencing as a red flag in transformation readiness assessments.
rationale: The proposed ISEA framework explicitly gives strategic architecture precedence, defines its directional role and explains that missing strategic scope produces technology-driven, misaligned investment. The CF accurately reflects the framework's sequencing principle.

authors: André, P.; Benjilany, A.; Bruneliere, H.; Tamzalit, D.
raw_condition_label: operational business-IT alignment requires continuous, multi-technique diagnostic assessment rather than a one-time check
readiness_statement: Because legacy information systems continuously accumulate incremental changes (technical debt, ad hoc adaptations, evolving business processes), operational business-IT alignment cannot be assessed once and assumed stable; it requires periodically repeated diagnostic assessment combining quantitative metrics (implementation/representation link counts and rates), qualitative consistency rules (cross-checking functional and data-dimension links), and anti-pattern detection (e.g., pure technical integration, functional silo, monolithic application, multiple functional implementations) to reveal areas of drift.
mechanism: Single-technique assessment (e.g., metrics alone) can mask or mis-signal misalignment -- e.g., a high rate of "unimplemented" business concepts may simply reflect composite/aggregated business processes rather than a true gap -- so triangulating multiple complementary diagnostic lenses reduces false positives/negatives and gives architects actionable, targeted evolution priorities rather than an undifferentiated alignment score.
operationalization_hint: Assess operational alignment using at least three complementary lenses -- coverage/implementation-rate metrics, cross-layer consistency rules, and anti-pattern catalogs -- and treat single-metric alignment scores as provisional until corroborated by the other lenses; automate detection via scripting where possible (e.g., jArchi over ArchiMate models) to make repeated reassessment practically sustainable.
rationale: The paper proposes an operational alignment evaluation that combines metrics, consistency rules and anti-pattern detection across functional and data dimensions. The CF accurately represents this multi-technique diagnostic approach.

readiness_statement: Organizations achieve IT-business strategic alignment not simply by adopting IT governance (ITG) mechanisms (decision-making structures, formal processes, communication approaches) but only when that adoption translates into genuine organizational commitment to the underlying principles of the ITG framework (e.g., COBIT's five principles: meeting stakeholder needs, end-to-end governance, an integrated evolving framework, a holistic approach, and separating governance from management). Commitment to ITG principles (CCP) fully mediates the relationship between ITG mechanism adoption and strategic alignment -- ITG mechanisms alone do not directly produce alignment.
mechanism: Mechanism adoption can be purely symbolic/instrumental ("following the letter" of governance rules without embracing their spirit/goals), which satisfies structural compliance but does not achieve the values-and-goals-based integration needed for genuine business-IT alignment; only when mechanism adoption is accompanied by felt commitment to the framework's underlying principles does IT become embedded in organizational objectives rather than treated as a separate function.
operationalization_hint: Assess not only whether ITG mechanisms (steering committees, formal processes, communication channels) are formally in place, but whether staff and leadership demonstrate committed endorsement of the governance framework's stated principles (e.g., via a validated CCP-style instrument); a validated CCP measure is provided in this paper and can be adapted to other principles-based frameworks (ISO/IEC 27001, ITIL, NIST, etc.).
rationale: The study reports full mediation of ITG mechanisms by commitment to COBIT principles for strategic alignment and distinguishes symbolic mechanism adoption from substantive commitment. The CF accurately captures the tested mediating relationship.

readiness_statement: Achieving IT-business strategic alignment requires support for IT from the full top leadership tier -- including the board of directors, not only C-level executives or IT management -- because top leadership support both strengthens organizational commitment to ITG principles and directly improves strategic alignment. ITG that remains a middle-management affair, without board and executive-level involvement, is unlikely to produce strategic alignment.
mechanism: When top leadership actively participates in IT vision and strategy (rather than passively endorsing it), it diffuses awareness of IT-related values, competencies, and governance principles throughout the firm, secures stakeholder buy-in, and helps overcome organizational resistance to IT-enabled change; because boards sit atop the firm's decision-making and governance hierarchy, their direct involvement (not just senior management's) is what confers legitimacy and centralized momentum to governance initiatives.
operationalization_hint: Measure top leadership support for IT as a construct spanning both board and executive-level participation (not top-management support alone, which is the common but incomplete operationalization in most prior IS research); readiness assessments should specifically check for documented board-level IT engagement, not just CIO/CEO sponsorship.
rationale: The paper defines top leadership support as board and executive participation in IT vision and strategy and reports its links to both commitment and strategic alignment. The CF accurately preserves this broader leadership construct.

Both individual relationships were also found to be curvilinear rather than simply linear.
mechanism: A plausible explanation is a substitutive relationship: heavily formalized, principles-based governance frameworks (like COBIT) may constrain leaders' ability to steer nimbly or lead by intuition, so when both principled commitment AND intense leadership steering are simultaneously very high, they may create friction or redundant/conflicting steering inputs rather than reinforcing one another; leaders lacking deep IT expertise may find highly formalized frameworks and highly assertive personal involvement to be competing rather than complementary steering mechanisms.
operationalization_hint: When evaluating governance-readiness conditions, do not assume leadership support and commitment to formal governance principles can simply be maximized independently; assess whether highly formalized governance and strong top-down steering are complementing each other or generating redundant, conflicting control pressure.
rationale: The study models CCP and top-leadership support as distinct influences and reports a non-additive moderation result. The CF appropriately records the finding as a governance-design boundary rather than a universal maximisation rule.

mechanism: Domain-specific models are built to reflect the concrete technological realities of a particular industrial context (e.g., Industry 4.0 manufacturing), which biases their dimension set toward technology and operations, whereas general models must abstract away from industry-specific technical detail and therefore lean on more universally applicable "soft" transformational dimensions -- meaning the choice of model type itself introduces a systematic assessment blind spot.
operationalization_hint: When selecting or adapting a maturity-assessment instrument, explicitly check whether it is domain-specific or general in origin, and supplement it with dimensions from the opposite category (technology/operations detail for general models; culture/leadership/governance depth for domain-specific models) to avoid a one-sided readiness picture.

authors: Magistretti, S.; Pham, C.T.A.; Dell'Era, C.
raw_condition_label: five design-thinking dynamic capabilities (extending, debating, cropping, interpreting, recombining) enable human-centered digital transformation by integrating technological and human perspectives
readiness_statement: Organizations pursuing digital transformation benefit from five specific design-thinking-rooted dynamic capabilities that translate ambiguous technological challenges into human-valued opportunities: (1) extending -- enlarging the shared knowledge base through close collaboration with diverse internal/external stakeholders; (2) debating -- juxtaposing digital/technological and human perspectives via critical questioning to reframe the challenge; (3) cropping -- selecting/retaining only the technological requirements and solution alternatives relevant to actual user needs, rather than being driven purely by data or technical functionality; (4) interpreting -- adopting different perceptual frames (e.g., distinct user archetypes/personas) to uncover new opportunities in the technology; and (5) recombining -- synthesizing technological and human/socio-cultural knowledge into a holistic solution framing.
mechanism: Standard dynamic-capability treatments of digital transformation (sensing/seizing/reconfiguring) are technology- and strategy-centered and risk producing digital solutions that are technically feasible but not meaningful or adopted by end users; design-thinking-rooted capabilities counterbalance this by embedding continuous empathizing, reframing, and synthesis activities throughout the technology-adoption process, ensuring that the opportunities provided by digital technologies result from harmonization with people's lives rather than treating the technology itself as the solution.
operationalization_hint: When running a digital-transformation initiative, explicitly assign process steps/roles for each of the five capabilities (e.g., structured stakeholder-extension sessions, dedicated debate/critique sessions contrasting technical vs. human framings, criteria-based cropping of requirements against user archetypes, and recombination workshops synthesizing technical and human insights) rather than relying on a generic "user research" phase alone.
rationale: The multiple-case study defines the five design-thinking dynamic capabilities and positions them as a human-centred complement to technology-focused digital transformation. The CF accurately represents the proposed capability set.

operationalization_hint: When designing a readiness-assessment governance artifact, build in a recurring reassessment trigger tied to competitive-environment monitoring (not just internal capability tracking), since a successful transformation changes the environment against which future readiness must be judged.

operationalization_hint: When sequencing a digital-transformation roadmap, prioritize organisational-culture and workforce-skill/well-being interventions ahead of major technological-infrastructure investment, and treat technology spend as conditional on people-readiness rather than a parallel or preceding track.
rationale: The study's abstract and conclusion identify culture, skills, engagement and well-being as people elements driving transformation and state that technological infrastructure should be invested in once these people elements are addressed.

operationalization_hint: Establish an ongoing technostress-monitoring track parallel to the technical rollout: identify likely technostressors (overload, invasion, insecurity, complexity) specific to the initiative, evaluate situational factors and design targeted interventions (e.g., structured training, clearer job-security communication, boundary-setting norms for remote work), and monitor employee strain levels continuously, especially during peak transformation activity.
rationale: The qualitative framework identifies job security and techno-invasion as technostress sources, calls for leadership measures, and recommends identifying and monitoring technostressors. The CF accurately frames technostress as an ongoing wellbeing risk.

raw_condition_label: employee negative emotional reactions to digital transformation are frequently misattributed as resistance to change, when they more often reflect protest against organizational inaction rather than resistance to the technology itself
readiness_statement: Across a large-sample survey (135 respondents, 44 municipalities) and interview study (24 respondents, 13 municipalities) on municipal digital transformation, sentiment analysis of interview transcripts found negative emotions (fear, frustration, anger) nearly balanced with positive emotions (41% vs. 49%), but qualitative follow-up discussion revealed that most of these negative emotions did not reflect employee resistance to change/technology itself; instead, they reflected dissatisfaction and protest at the organization's failure to act (absence of strategy, structure, or support for digital transformation) -- a fundamentally different diagnosis with different remediation implications.
mechanism: Coding raw sentiment as "negative = resistance to change" without deeper qualitative interpretation risks misdiagnosing the actual barrier; in this study, employees expressing anger or frustration were often protesting the lack of organizational digital-transformation activity (no structure, no strategic plan, no training) rather than opposing change itself -- meaning organizations that interpret negative employee sentiment as resistance-to-technology and respond with change-management/persuasion tactics may be addressing the wrong problem, when the actual fix needed is organizational action (providing structure, strategy, and resources), not overcoming employee reluctance.
operationalization_hint: When negative employee sentiment toward digital transformation is detected, do not automatically categorize it as "resistance to change"; use follow-up qualitative probing to correctly diagnose whether the barrier is organizational inaction or genuine resistance, since the appropriate remediation differs substantially between the two.
rationale: The municipal study reports near-balanced positive and negative sentiment and, after discussion with respondents, finds that most negative emotions reflected protest at unaddressed organisational conditions rather than resistance to change itself. It explicitly warns that sentiment alone would misinterpret the behaviour.

rationale: The validated municipal barrier framework records absence of data management as 90 references or 18% of coded barriers. The CF accurately reports this context-specific quantitative predominance.

readiness_statement: Across 36 companies spanning four industrial sectors, zero companies reached the highest "Digital Transformation" readiness level (level 5 of 5); readiness instead clustered at "Not existent" (24.6%), "Basic digital operation" (21.5%), "Advanced digital operation" (30.7%), and "Digital integration" (23.2%). mechanism: Achieving full digital transformation requires simultaneous, sustained maturity across people, process, technology, and innovation dimensions, which is disproportionately difficult for smaller or less digitally-invested firms that lack the resource base to advance all four dimensions in parallel; larger firms and those investing a higher share of turnover in digital technologies can sustain broader, more parallel capability development, producing the observed graded relationship between resource commitment/scale and readiness level.
operationalization_hint: When benchmarking a firm's digital-transformation readiness, calibrate expectations against firm size and digital-investment intensity (e.g., percentage of turnover) rather than against an absolute "fully transformed" target, since even well-resourced firms in a broad cross-sector sample rarely if ever reach complete transformation.

authors: Dang-Pham, D.; Hoang, A.-P.; Vo, D.-T.; Kautz, K.
raw_condition_label: decomposing large-scale digital transformation into small, quick-win projects resolving cross-functional pain points (identified via structured, mandatory cross-departmental workshops) builds transformation momentum incrementally
readiness_statement: Rather than pursuing "big-bang" disruption, successful large-scale digital transformation can be decomposed into a repeatable six-step cycle (discover improvement potential, analyse current work, generate ideas, develop/implement, evaluate) applied to small, cross-functional "pain points" identified through regular, mandatory workshops attended by managers from all departments, with each resulting project capped at strict time (e.g., 6-month) and evaluation (feasibility, urgency, strategic value) criteria; visible, fast wins from these small projects build employee morale and management trust, which in turn increases participation in subsequent transformation initiatives.
mechanism: Framing digital transformation as one large, uncertain, resource-intensive program tends to make managers hesitant or resistant, especially in SMEs and even large enterprises facing scope-creep risk; by contrast, decomposing the transformation into small, time-boxed projects that solve problems employees actually experience day-to-day (rather than top-down mandated initiatives) produces fast, visible, and attributable wins, and these visible successes create a self-reinforcing cycle of trust and morale that lowers resistance to the next round of change.

raw_condition_label: balanced technology and human-capital investment (not technology investment alone) predicts digital-transformation goal achievement
readiness_statement: A study of 3,146 firms found that only firms making balanced investments in both technology and human-capital development achieved their targeted digital-transformation goals; firms investing heavily in technology without corresponding human-capital investment achieved only about 40% of their targeted outcomes.
mechanism: Technology deployed without matching investment in workforce skills, change management, and talent development lacks the human capacity to actually operate, adapt, or extend the new digital capability, so the technology investment's realized value is capped well below its potential regardless of its technical sophistication.
operationalization_hint: When allocating a DT budget, require an explicit, tracked allocation to human-capital development (training, talent acquisition, change management) proportional to the technology investment, rather than treating technology spend as the primary or sole budget line.
rationale: The review reports that the 3,146-firm study found target achievement only for balanced technology and human-capital investment. The CF accurately preserves the stated balance condition.

raw_condition_label: three complementary theoretical lenses (digital maturity model, Industry 4.0, dynamic capabilities theory) map to distinct, jointly-necessary resilience dimensions
readiness_statement: A comprehensive resilience-through-DT assessment should combine three theoretical lenses that each capture a distinct resilience dimension: the digital maturity model for preparedness and adaptive capacity (data-driven insight, customer-centric cultural readiness), the Industry 4.0 framework for response capability and operational efficiency (IoT/AI/cyber-physical integration), and dynamic capabilities theory for recovery and strategic flexibility (resource sensing, seizing, and reconfiguration) -- using only one lens leaves at least one resilience dimension unassessed.
mechanism: Each framework was independently developed to explain a different slice of organizational response to change (readiness posture, operational-technology integration, and strategic resource reconfiguration respectively); because real disruptions test all three simultaneously, an assessment or roadmap grounded in only one framework will miss the conditions the other two frameworks are best suited to diagnose.
operationalization_hint: When designing a DT-for-resilience roadmap, deliberately map planned initiatives against all three dimensions (preparedness/adaptive capacity, response capability/efficiency, recovery/strategic flexibility) rather than defaulting to whichever single framework is most familiar to the assessment team.
rationale: The review framework explicitly combines governance, technological readiness and innovation ecosystems as resilience dimensions. The CF accurately turns the multi-lens framework into an assessment practice.

raw_condition_label: top-management leadership importance exceeding formal DT-strategy formalization as a success condition
readiness_statement: Across two independently analyzed large-company case studies (insurance, manufacturing), consistent top-management (C-level) leadership that internalizes DT as a pervasive business initiative -- not the existence of a separate, formally documented DT strategy -- was the more decisive success condition; both companies succeeded with only lightly formalized (or entirely informal, "in the head of" a single executive) DT strategies.
mechanism: An explicitly formalized strategy mainly helps pre-digital, less digitally mature organizations check strategic fit and communicate goals broadly; once a credible top-management champion (e.g., a CIO acting as informal CDO) has internalized and consistently communicated the DT direction, the coordinating function of a written strategy document becomes less necessary.
operationalization_hint: Assess whether a credible, consistently-engaged top-management champion exists and is trusted to communicate DT direction, rather than checking only for the existence of a written DT strategy document.

rationale: The comparative case-study conclusion explicitly prioritizes C-level leadership that embeds DT as a business initiative over formal DT strategic planning.

raw_condition_label: digital governance and leadership as twin, distinct enablers (policy/accountability structures vs. vision/culture-inspiring leadership) of digital transformation maturity
readiness_statement: Digital governance (policies, structures, processes, and mechanisms establishing accountability and prioritization for digital initiatives) and digital leadership (vision, culture, and mindset that inspires innovation, collaboration, and agility) are conceptually distinct enablers of digital maturity, not a single "leadership" construct; without governance, DT efforts lack direction and compatibility with business objectives even if leaders are personally inspiring, while without inspiring leadership, governance structures alone fail to motivate genuine employee participation.
mechanism: Governance supplies the formal coordination and prioritization mechanism (which initiatives get resourced, how risk/compliance is managed), while leadership supplies the motivational and cultural mechanism (why employees should embrace change); an organization strong in one but weak in the other experiences either well-resourced-but-uninspired initiatives or enthusiastic-but-uncoordinated ones.
operationalization_hint: Assess digital governance (formal policies/accountability for digital initiatives) and digital leadership (vision-communication and culture-building capacity) as two separate readiness dimensions rather than folding them into one "leadership" item.
canonical_label: Dedicated digital leadership roles with real authority
cluster_label: Dedicated digital leadership roles with real authority
rationale: The study defines governance through policies, structures, processes, and coordination, while describing leadership as vision, culture, and motivation; the finding appropriately treats them as distinct but jointly relevant enablers.

raw_condition_label: digital maturity stage typology contrasting technology-capability strength against leadership-capability strength (beginners/enthusiasts/conservatives/leaders)
readiness_statement: Organizations progressing toward digital maturity fall into distinct failure/success archetypes depending on whether they are strong in technological capability, leadership/governance capability, both, or neither: "digital enthusiasts" over-invest in every new digital tool but lack governance/coordination and therefore waste resources on non-adaptive, uncoordinated systems; "digital conservatives" have strong governance/leadership discipline but excessive caution prevents them from building powerful technological capabilities; only "digital leaders" excel at both and achieve superior results.
mechanism: Because technology adoption and leadership/governance capability can develop independently of each other, assessing only one (e.g., counting adopted technologies) misses organizations that are technologically active but organizationally incoherent, or vice versa; the two-axis typology exposes which specific combination of strengths and gaps an organization has.
operationalization_hint: When benchmarking an organization's digital maturity, plot it on both a technology-capability axis and a leadership/governance-capability axis rather than a single composite score, to correctly diagnose whether the binding constraint is technological or organizational.
rationale: The maturity typology explicitly distinguishes beginners, enthusiasts, conservatives, and leaders through contrasting technology and leadership/governance capability profiles.

readiness_statement: Digital transformation maturity assessment models developed for developed-country contexts are not directly transferable to developing countries because measurable maturity there must also account for a distinct "digital divide" progression (infrastructure access, skills, and outcomes) shaped by socioeconomic and cultural inequality factors (income, education, welfare, culture) not present as binding constraints in developed-economy models.
mechanism: Standard maturity dimensions (organization, technology, strategy, employees, customers, processes, culture) implicitly assume a baseline of infrastructure access and digital literacy that cannot be assumed in developing-country contexts, so an additional digital-divide-stage assessment is needed to correctly locate an organization's actual starting point.
operationalization_hint: When building or selecting a maturity assessment for a developing-country organization, add explicit digital-divide-stage items (infrastructure access, skills, outcomes) alongside the standard dimensions.
rationale: The maturity-model study explicitly frames the digital divide and developing-country context as relevant to maturity assessment, including infrastructure, skills, and socioeconomic context. The CF appropriately records a transferability boundary and an added assessment requirement for this context.

raw_condition_label: single-assessor digital maturity self-assessment risks systematic optimism bias from higher-hierarchy respondents; interdisciplinary, multi-level assessor panels are needed for accurate maturity scoring
readiness_statement: Experts who pilot-tested the DSTM assessment model explicitly flagged that not all aspects of digital maturity can be accurately assessed by one person, and that employees at higher levels of hierarchy tend to assess digital maturity more optimistically than employees at lower levels, meaning a single-assessor or management-only assessment process risks systematically overstating actual digital maturity.
mechanism: Senior respondents may have more visibility into strategic intent and less exposure to day-to-day execution friction than lower-hierarchy employees, biasing their self-assessment upward relative to the on-the-ground reality that lower-level employees experience directly.
operationalization_hint: Require digital maturity self-assessments to be completed by an interdisciplinary panel spanning multiple hierarchical levels (not just senior management), and treat single-respondent or management-only assessment scores as likely optimistic upper bounds rather than accurate current-state measures.
rationale: The authors report assessors' limitation that one person cannot assess all aspects and recommend an interdisciplinary, multi-hierarchy assessment group because senior staff may assess maturity more optimistically.

readiness_statement: A systematic review of 22 existing digital maturity models found that the aspect of developing new digital business models is hardly addressed in almost any of them, and this gap was confirmed empirically in the pilot test, where "Digital Service Business Model" subfactors (framework, ecosystem) scored among the lowest of all Digital Impact factors even in companies that scored well on "Service Engineering & Innovation".
mechanism: Because most existing maturity models were developed with a technology-exploitation lens (assessing how well an organisation deploys and integrates digital tools), they systematically under-instrument the exploration-oriented capability of designing genuinely new digital business models and ecosystems, so organisations relying on these models to guide their DT roadmap will underinvest in business-model innovation relative to technology deployment.
operationalization_hint: When selecting or building a digital maturity assessment, explicitly check whether it includes dedicated business-model and digital-ecosystem-design criteria, since most existing models (and organisations following them) systematically underweight this dimension relative to technology and process dimensions.
rationale: The review of 22 maturity models finds digital business models hardly addressed; the pilot further shows low maturity for the business-model framework and ecosystem subfactors.

raw_condition_label: customer centricity, innovation process, value creation, and organisational agility rank as the most impactful DT-readiness enablers, while competitive-positioning and data-management rank lowest
readiness_statement: Among Rogers' (2016) six DT-readiness enablers, an expert panel across six Portuguese organisations rated Customer Centricity, Innovation Process, Value Creation, and Organisational Agility as the most impactful for DT readiness, while Competitive Positioning (inter-firm digital-platform collaboration) and Data Management scored notably lower and were considered less of a priority.
mechanism: The four highest-rated enablers all center on internally-controllable, customer- and process-facing capabilities that organisations can develop unilaterally, whereas Competitive Positioning requires trust and collaboration with external, potentially competing parties, and Data Management requires organisation-wide data accessibility that may conflict with data-sensitivity concerns -- both introducing dependencies or risks the four top-rated enablers do not.
operationalization_hint: When prioritizing DT-readiness investments with limited resources, favor customer-centricity, innovation-process, value-creation, and organisational-agility initiatives first, and treat inter-firm data/platform collaboration and organisation-wide data accessibility as secondary unless the specific industry context favors them.

mechanism: The replication approach treats existing validated tools as the starting point (technology-first), while the process approach treats identified business problems as the starting point (problem-first); each approach's weakness is the other's strength, so combining them lets an organisation start delivering quick wins from replication while a parallel diagnostic effort surfaces problems replication alone would miss.
operationalization_hint: When designing a DT program roadmap, explicitly decide whether to lead with proven-tool replication (for speed) or full process diagnostics (for thoroughness), or run both in a deliberately synchronized parallel track rather than defaulting to only one.
rationale: The paper explicitly contrasts a top-down replication approach with a bottom-up diagnostic approach, identifies their respective limitations, and states that synchronized parallel use is possible.

mechanism: Because off-the-shelf Industry 4.0 technologies still require customization and sometimes R&D effort to fit a specific industrial context (per the TRL-context-dependency finding above), and large enterprises can absorb this cost through dedicated R&D functions while SMEs cannot, the same nominal technology-adoption task represents a categorically larger readiness barrier for SMEs than for large enterprises.
operationalization_hint: When assessing or supporting SME digital transformation readiness, budget explicitly for customization/R&D effort as a distinct SME-specific cost category, and consider public support programs, digital maturity audits, or collaborative innovation ecosystems as compensating mechanisms rather than assuming SMEs can absorb this burden as easily as large enterprises.

raw_condition_label: communicating change from stakeholders' individual frame of reference reduces emotional resistance that purely cognitive project methodologies (PMBOK, Scrum) do not address
readiness_statement: Standard project and agile methodologies (PMBOK, Scrum) engage stakeholders' cognitive processes (planning, adaptive problem-solving) but do not address the emotional uncertainty people feel when facing change; explicitly understanding and communicating from each stakeholder's individual Frame of Reference (FOR) -- their existing beliefs, concerns, and reasoning -- rather than arguing facts, is what converts resistance into engagement.
mechanism: People react to change with both cognitive and emotional responses; when a Change Agent listens to and reflects a stakeholder's FOR back to them without judgment, the stakeholder feels understood and shifts from defending a position to exploring their own thoughts and motives, which reduces resistance more effectively than presenting additional facts or logical arguments.
operationalization_hint: Before or alongside standard requirements-gathering and sprint-planning activities, have a designated change agent map each stakeholder group's frame of reference (concerns, incentives, prior experience with similar changes) and tailor communication content and channel to that frame rather than using one uniform message.

rationale: The framework contrasts the cognitive focus of PMBOK and Scrum with emotional responses to uncertainty and prescribes communication from stakeholders' Frame of Reference without judgment.

raw_condition_label: organizational core values act as an implicit interpretive filter connecting vision to digital transformation decisions, though vision documents themselves risk being perceived as non-functional "window dressing"
readiness_statement: In two of three case organizations, core cultural values (e.g., a local government's stated commitment to "openness and transparency") were found to actively shape how vision-derived desired results were elaborated and pursued, demonstrating that values function as a live interpretive filter on strategic sensing -- yet in the same organization, the CIO explicitly questioned whether the published vision was authentic guidance or "just meant as window dressing to make us look better," while a factory-automation strategy manager treated the mission/vision as a genuine and consistently invoked starting point for all change initiatives.
mechanism: Vision statements only function as effective sensing-capability inputs when stakeholders perceive them as authentic and operative rather than as marketing artifacts; core values appear to be a more consistently trusted and operative guide across organizations than formally documented vision statements, suggesting values may be a more reliable EA-information input than vision documents in organizations where vision credibility is in question.
operationalization_hint: When using EA vision/mission artifacts to drive digital transformation sensing, first verify (e.g., via stakeholder interviews) whether the vision is perceived internally as authentic strategic guidance or as symbolic messaging, and supplement or substitute it with documented core organizational values where vision credibility is low.

raw_condition_label: closeness of a digital activity to the core business, combined with its exploration-versus-exploitation classification, should jointly drive the decision to separate or integrate it structurally
readiness_statement: Across 33 interviews spanning multiple industries and hierarchy levels, the decision to structurally separate versus integrate a digital initiative is best driven by two joint criteria: (1) whether the activity is exploratory (radical, future-oriented, high-risk) or exploitative (incremental, efficiency-focused, using existing products/processes) and (2) how close the activity is to the core business; distant exploration should be separated (e.g., in an innovation hub, think tank, or spun-off unit), while exploitation close to the core should be integrated, with exploration close to the core admitting either option depending on additional risk factors.
mechanism: Distant exploration needs freedom, dedicated budget, and different processes/culture that a core organization's follow-up-oriented, efficiency-focused culture would suppress, whereas exploitation requires deep process/product/customer knowledge that only exists within the core organization, so applying the wrong structural choice in either direction either stifles innovation or produces solutions disconnected from real business needs.
operationalization_hint: Before deciding whether to structurally separate a digital initiative, explicitly classify it on two axes -- exploration vs. exploitation, and closeness to the core business -- and use the resulting quadrant (not intuition or a blanket "digital vs. non-digital" split) to decide on separation, integration, or a hybrid approach with safeguards.
rationale: The 33-interview study states that separation/integration depends on exploration or exploitation and closeness to the core, recommending separation for distant exploration and integration for core-connected exploitation.

raw_condition_label: separating all digital activities from the core business (rather than distinguishing exploration from exploitation) risks creating perceived injustice and starving the core business of digital skills and mindset transfer
readiness_statement: Separating all digital activities from the core business as a blanket strategy (e.g., to build a digital mentality via M&A or internal startup culture) creates a risk that the digital unit is favored over the core business -- perceived as receiving investment, new office spaces, and prestige while the core business is "asked for more EBIT" -- generating a sense of injustice, and can leave the core organization permanently "in the non-digital world" because knowledge about new technologies and digital mindsets never transfers back.
mechanism: Blanket separation conflates exploration (which genuinely benefits from separation) with exploitation (which needs integration), so activities that should have been integrated get isolated instead, cutting off the knowledge-transfer and cultural-diffusion channels the core business needs to digitize its own processes, while simultaneously creating a two-tier status system between "favored" digital staff and "legacy" core staff.
operationalization_hint: Before separating all digital activity into a dedicated unit, explicitly distinguish which of those activities are exploration (appropriate for separation) versus exploitation (which should remain integrated or closely linked), and establish deliberate knowledge-transfer mechanisms back to the core business regardless of the chosen structure.
page_or_section: Results section (Organizational separation: Digital/Core business), Discussion
rationale: The findings identify favoritism and perceived injustice risks from digital/core separation and state that weak links prevent digital knowledge and mindsets transferring to the core business.

raw_condition_label: digital maturity grade functions as a temporal trigger for re-evaluating separation/integration decisions: early-stage transformation favors separation to build digital literacy, while increasing maturity favors integration
readiness_statement: The digital maturity grade of an incumbent company acts as a trigger point for rethinking organizational separation decisions: early in a digital transformation, separating digital activities helps generate a startup culture and build digital literacy that does not yet exist internally, but as the company matures and grows closer to the core business, the pull for digital improvements in the core business increases, becoming a trigger to dissolve or integrate the previously separate digital hub.
mechanism: Early separation solves a bootstrapping problem (lack of internal digital knowledge/culture), but that same separation becomes counterproductive once digital capability has matured, because continued separation at that stage blocks exactly the core-business integration and efficiency gains the company set out to capture -- meaning the optimal organizational structure is not fixed but should be re-evaluated as maturity increases.
operationalization_hint: Treat organizational separation/integration decisions as time-bound, not permanent: schedule periodic re-assessment of digital maturity grade specifically as a trigger to revisit whether a previously separated digital unit should now be integrated into the core business.
rationale: The results identify digital maturity grade as a trigger to reconsider separation: early separation builds literacy and startup culture, whereas greater maturity and core-business pull trigger hub dissolution/integration.

readiness_statement: Organizations typically approach strategic topics by first defining their strategy and then identifying the capabilities needed to achieve it, but DMMs frequently reverse this sequence by prescribing the capabilities required to meet a predefined (often peer-group-derived) target maturity state that the organization cannot easily adjust -- creating a structural mismatch between the organization's own strategy-formulation logic and the DMM's built-in logic that was identified as a specific barrier to DMM adoption.

operationalization_hint: Before applying a DMM as a steering tool, explicitly reconcile its prescribed target-state capabilities with the organization's own strategy-first goal-setting process, and be prepared to adapt or reinterpret DMM benchmarks rather than treating them as a substitute for organization-specific goal derivation.

readiness_statement: A two-round Delphi study (53 experts, Kendall's W=0.51) demonstrates that digital transformation readiness is better captured as a configurational pattern of how strategic attention is allocated across seven interdependent domains (Competition, Customer, Data, Innovation, Regulation, Technology, Value) than as an additive/compensatory composite score, because in interdependent systems underdevelopment in one domain constrains the effectiveness of investments in others -- meaning strength in one domain cannot substitute for weakness in another, contrary to the compensatory logic implicit in most maturity models and composite readiness indices.
mechanism: Additive/compensatory scoring assumes domains are independent contributors to an overall score, but complementarity theory shows that the marginal return on investment in one domain depends on the development level of related domains, so an organization can appear "digitally mature" in aggregate while having a critical, unaddressed imbalance that a compensatory score would mask entirely.
operationalization_hint: When designing or interpreting any digital transformation readiness/maturity assessment, avoid producing a single aggregated score; instead, report and interpret domain-level scores as a distribution/profile, explicitly flagging domains that are low relative to their structural importance rather than allowing high scores elsewhere to offset them.
rationale: The SFI explicitly adopts a non-compensatory domain-profile logic, stating that under-emphasis in one structurally interdependent domain cannot be offset by strength in others; the Delphi reports W approximately .51.

mechanism: Because domains are interdependent, a domain's low relative priority reflects its role as an enabling/constraining boundary condition rather than a primary value-creation lever; removing attention to it entirely (rather than proportionally reducing it) risks removing a necessary condition for the higher-priority domains to function, which a simple ranked-priority list could obscure.
operationalization_hint: When using any domain-prioritization framework to allocate digital transformation resources, retain a baseline minimum investment in low-weighted but structurally necessary domains (e.g., regulatory compliance, competitive monitoring) rather than deprioritizing them to zero, even when they rank last in strategic-attention weight.
