raw_condition_label: organizational agility for digital transformation manifests as two structurally opposite but equally valid paths: liquid/project-based dissolution of departments versus stable hierarchy with new agility-specific roles layered in
readiness_statement: Across 16 expert interviews, organizational agility for digital transformation was described in two distinct, non-overlapping ways: (1) a "liquid organisation" path that dissolves classical departments and functions in favor of project-oriented, competency-based grouping with leaders acting as moderators rather than supervisors, and (2) a stable, hierarchical organisation that retains its classical organisational chart but layers in new agility-enabling roles (e.g., data scientist, community manager, digital consultant) to inject quick-response capability without restructuring.
mechanism: Both paths achieve the same underlying goal -- faster response to market opportunities and changing circumstances -- through different mechanisms: the liquid path removes structural friction by eliminating departmental boundaries entirely, while the role-injection path adds specialized quick-response capacity into an otherwise unchanged structure, meaning organizations do not have to choose between "agile" and "traditional" as a binary but can select the path matching their risk tolerance for restructuring.
operationalization_hint: When assessing or designing organizational agility for digital transformation, do not assume agility requires abandoning hierarchy; consider whether a targeted new-roles approach within the existing structure could achieve comparable responsiveness with lower disruption than a full liquid-organization redesign.

operationalization_hint: When assessing an organization's "culture of change" readiness, explicitly distinguish whether the goal is evolutionary failure-tolerance (a necessary but lower-intensity precondition) or disruptive structural reorientation (a more intensive, less common transformation), since these require different interventions and should not be conflated in a single culture-readiness score.

raw_condition_label: surge capacity cultivated during stability enables absorption of environmental disruption shocks
readiness_statement: Organizations that build surge capacity -- the ability to rapidly mobilize, redeploy, and scale resources -- during periods of relative operational stability are better positioned to absorb sudden environmental shocks (e.g., COVID-19, regulatory change, competitive disruption) without compromising service delivery or losing transformation momentum.
mechanism: Surge capacity is not built reactively during a crisis; it is accumulated in advance through resource slack and redeployable capabilities during stable periods, so that when disruption hits, the organization can compress decision cycles and reallocate resources rapidly instead of being paralyzed by the shock (illustrated by low-cost carriers' sub-30-minute turnaround capability).
operationalization_hint: Assess whether the organization maintains redeployable resource slack and rapid-reallocation routines during non-crisis periods, not only its crisis-response playbooks.
rationale: The paper frames surge capacity as the ability to mobilize, redeploy, and scale resources under unpredictable disruptions, and explicitly positions it as necessary to balance stability and change.

raw_condition_label: digital transformation resources simultaneously enable capability and generate new organizational fragility (resource-capability paradox)
readiness_statement: IT infrastructure, human capital, and resource-management systems that resolve pre-existing inefficiencies during DT simultaneously introduce new dependencies, coordination burdens, and single points of failure, so that DT resources do not reduce organizational complexity but redistribute it, requiring ongoing managerial attention rather than one-time investment.
mechanism: As systems grow more integrated and complex (e.g., ERP overhauls, centralized knowledge platforms), failures become harder to diagnose and more disruptive, and skill-building initiatives that close technical gaps simultaneously open new generational/cultural divides -- so every resource investment that increases capability also increases the surface area for fragility.
operationalization_hint: When assessing resource adequacy for DT readiness, evaluate not only whether resources exist but what new dependencies, failure points, or coordination burdens each resource investment creates.
rationale: The article explicitly identifies increased fragility and coordination challenges alongside improvements in speed, integration, and flexibility, supporting the resource-capability paradox.

operationalization_hint: Track resistance patterns as a diagnostic signal (which employees, which tasks) rather than only as an adoption-rate metric to suppress.
rationale: The study reports internal testing before launch as confidence-building while noting that collaborative processes can slow decisions, and explicitly frames resistance as a signal of capability gaps. This supports the diagnostic and tension-oriented CF.

readiness_statement: Digital transformation readiness should be understood not as the static presence of enabling conditions (leadership commitment, cultural readiness, external pressure) but as the capacity of these conditions to catalytically trigger a shift from resource exploitation to capability reconfiguration when activated -- organizations with similar resource endowments can experience divergent transformation trajectories depending on whether enabling conditions actually activate this shift.
mechanism: Enabling factors do not resolve organizational tensions when present; they function as catalysts that force organizations to question existing value-creation logic and identity claims, and their catalytic effect (rather than their mere presence) is what differentiates transformation trajectories across otherwise similarly-resourced organizations.
operationalization_hint: Assess readiness by asking whether enabling conditions have historically triggered actual capability-reconfiguration episodes in the organization, not merely whether they are nominally present (e.g., a documented DT strategy, a culture survey score).
rationale: The theoretical framing defines leadership commitment, supportive culture, and external pressure as catalysts for resource-to-capability shifts rather than merely static resource conditions.

mechanism: Cultural and strategic readiness (leadership commitment, openness to change) can be built through low-cost internal effort, whereas data-analytics, cybersecurity, and advanced-technology capability require capital investment and specialized skills that resource-constrained SMEs systematically underinvest in, producing a durable, structural (not incidental) maturity gap between soft and technical dimensions.
operationalization_hint: When assessing SME transformation readiness, expect and specifically probe technical/analytical dimensions (data, cybersecurity, advanced tech) as the binding constraint even where cultural/strategic dimensions score well.
rationale: The SME results report substantially higher culture/skills and customer scores than Data & Analytics and Industry 4.0/advanced technology scores, establishing the stated asymmetry.

raw_condition_label: absence of a consensual, cross-sector digital transformation maturity model as a caveat/gap condition
readiness_statement: Across 15 major digital maturity models (147 total variables, mapped onto the six Archimate 3.0 EA layers), none covers all six layers: 14 of 15 models address the Strategy and Business layers and most address Application, but only 6 of 15 partially address the Technology layer, and none addresses the Physical or Implementation-and-Migration layers at all -- creating a systematic assessment blind spot in precisely the technical/implementation layers that originate and support digitization.
mechanism: Maturity-model developers have concentrated on business-side dimensions (strategy, culture, customer experience) because these are more universally applicable and easier to survey across organizations, leaving the more implementation-specific and heterogeneous technical layers (infrastructure, migration) systematically under-modeled despite digitization being technologically driven.
operationalization_hint: When selecting or composing a digital maturity assessment instrument, explicitly check which EA layers it covers and supplement with a technology/infrastructure-layer-specific instrument if the chosen model stops at Strategy/Business/Application.
rationale: The 15-model analysis finds no model able to cover all architecture layers and reports that Physical and Implementation/Migration layers are absent while technical coverage is limited.

raw_condition_label: traditional waterfall, IT-focused enterprise architecture practice is structurally mismatched with digital-transformation demands for agile, business-focused, ecosystem-oriented planning
readiness_statement: Traditional EA practice -- rooted in IT, using a waterfall development approach, organized around organizational/integration/software/infrastructure layers, and targeting IT-architect audiences -- is structurally mismatched with digital-transformation requirements for business-focus, agile/iterative development, strategic and business-model-layer integration, and ecosystem/platform-oriented value creation; this mismatch is a key reason EA remains largely unused and poorly understood in SME digital-transformation practice.
mechanism: Because EA and business-transformation disciplines originate in different fields with different languages, description techniques, and target audiences, EA's IT-rooted vocabulary and detailed-upfront-planning approach create a genuine translation gap with the customer-integrated, fast-iterating, ecosystem-spanning practices digital transformation demands, rather than EA simply being underused due to lack of awareness.
operationalization_hint: When assessing whether EA can support a specific digital-transformation initiative, check whether the EA approach in use has been adapted toward business-focus, agility, and ecosystem/platform layers, rather than assuming a traditional/IT-focused EA practice will transfer directly.

raw_condition_label: agile enterprise architecture macro/micro-cycle method (architecture backlog) as an operationalization for SME digital-transformation planning
readiness_statement: SME digital-transformation planning can be operationalized as a macro cycle (defining and incrementally refining the whole-enterprise architecture, from an unconstrained 'ideal architecture' toward a legacy-constrained 'real architecture') paired with a micro cycle (implementing and testing individual capsuled 'user stories' drawn from an architecture backlog, analogous to a Scrum product backlog), allowing agile, incremental EA development instead of upfront, complete architecture specification.
mechanism: Deriving an unconstrained ideal architecture first (without legacy or resource restrictions) and only then reconciling it against the real, legacy-constrained architecture prevents premature anchoring on existing systems, while decomposing the gap into independently-runnable, prioritized user stories (the architecture backlog) lets small SME teams make incremental progress without needing to complete a full upfront architecture before starting implementation.

raw_condition_label: EAM governance/control-mechanism portfolios must be dynamically reconfigured to match situational context: crisis/scarcity favors formal top-down control, while stability-with-innovation-focus favors informal, relational control
readiness_statement: Across three distinct decade-long strategic episodes at a major international bank (2008 financial crisis and merger integration; 2012-2016 core-IT modernization; 2016-2018 digital-technology-company strategic pivot), the effective EAM control-mechanism portfolio shifted from predominantly formal, top-down modes (input and behavioural control: architectural task forces, mandated blueprints, management oversight) during the crisis/scarcity episode, toward increasingly informal, relational modes (clan control, self-control: networking activities, voluntary team engagement, joint architectural discussions) during the later stability-and-innovation-focused episodes -- with each shift explicitly triggered by a major strategic realignment.
mechanism: Formal control mechanisms (resource allocation, behaviour monitoring, output tracking) can be established quickly and produce nearly immediate effects, which is valuable when resources are scarce, environmental uncertainty is high, and a clear target exists (e.g., merger integration under financial-crisis pressure); informal control mechanisms (shared norms, intrinsic motivation, voluntary engagement) take longer to build effects but are better suited to situations with less resource pressure and more emphasis on innovation, exploration, and buy-in, where clear a priori targets and detailed roadmaps are not yet available.
operationalization_hint: When designing or diagnosing an EA governance approach, first characterize the current situational context (crisis/scarcity vs. stability/innovation-focus) and select the emphasis of the control-mechanism portfolio (formal vs. informal) accordingly, rather than applying one EAM governance style uniformly regardless of context.

readiness_statement: Enterprise architecture initiatives spanning multiple organizations (extended enterprise architecture, EEA) are jointly influenced by six analytically distinct factors: precision (how precisely stakeholders, strategy, and mutual obligations are defined), imbalance (power asymmetry between partner organizations, e.g., customers typically holding more power than suppliers), heterogeneity (organizational and technological differences between stakeholders, sometimes requiring standards adoption), transformation (the need for artifact-translation mechanisms between differing stakeholder architectures), temporality (the relationship's lifecycle, duration, and synchronization requirements, illustrated by relationships lasting from months to 20+ years), and maturity (operational stability and continuous-improvement capability once the EEA reaches a steady state) -- illustrated through a real case of a European fashion trading company managing distinct EEA relationships with online retailers, department stores, and tax authorities.
mechanism: Because a single-enterprise EA framework implicitly assumes one authoritative strategy-setting entity, extending EA across organizational boundaries introduces six qualitatively new sources of friction (imprecise mutual obligations, asymmetric power, heterogeneous legacy systems, translation needs between differing architectures, divergent relationship lifecycles, and varying operational maturity across partners) that a single-enterprise EA framework has no native mechanism to address, explaining why generic EA frameworks extended informally to multi-organization contexts frequently underperform.
operationalization_hint: When assessing EA readiness for a transformation initiative that spans multiple organizations, explicitly evaluate all six factors (precision, imbalance, heterogeneity, transformation, temporality, maturity) rather than assuming single-enterprise EA practices transfer directly to the multi-organization context.
rationale: The extended-enterprise discussion identifies precision, imbalance, heterogeneity, transformation, temporality, and maturity as the key notions shaping cross-enterprise EA.

readiness_statement: Enterprise architecture (EA) and project portfolio management (PPM) address complementary but distinct scopes -- EA determines technical goals and constraints (IT requirements, legacy/platform/interoperability limitations) scoped to IT projects, while PPM determines organizational goals and constraints (budget, resources, capacity, business-change initiatives) scoped to all strategic change initiatives across the enterprise -- and a systematic literature review found that most prior strategic-alignment models include one of these two functions but omit the other, indicating that EA-PPM connectivity is chronically underestimated in both theory and practice.
mechanism: Because EA lacks the organizational/business-portfolio view needed to capture business-IT relations at the whole-enterprise level, and PPM lacks the technical perspective needed to implement IT strategies, decision-making conducted within either function's silo alone (without deliberately exchanging technical and organizational analyses) will systematically miss either technical feasibility constraints or organizational resource/priority constraints.
operationalization_hint: When assessing IT-project or transformation-initiative readiness, verify that EA's technical-goal analysis and PPM's organizational-goal analysis are both being conducted and are being explicitly exchanged, not merely that one or the other function exists.

mechanism: Because organizations are complex adaptive systems where symptom-only correction produces short-term improvement followed by long-term performance degradation, treating EA design as the rational top-down component and coevolutionary sensing/governance/prevention as the emergent bottom-up component lets the organization reconcile top-down control with bottom-up adaptation across both short-term and long-term time horizons.

rationale: The coevolutionary framework explicitly comprises EA design, misalignment sensing, governance, and prevention, distinguishing short-term governance from long-term prevention principles.

rationale: The model explains EA value realization through conversion factors, appropriate use, and conditions; it identifies management, communication, team, framework, vision, and governance as conversion influences.

mechanism: A single-dimension or narrowly-scoped readiness checklist (e.g., prior MPS assessments covering only 4 or 9 factors) fails to capture the holistic people/process/technology/catalyst view that EA scholars recommend; consolidating factors from systematic review and expert interviews into 4 elements, then validating them through 3 rounds of Delphi consensus (IQR 0-1, median 4-5 on all 45 items), produces a comprehensive and expert-endorsed readiness taxonomy.
operationalization_hint: Before EA establishment, score readiness separately against all four elements (Catalyst Enabler, People, Process, Technology) rather than a single composite index, to identify which specific element is the binding constraint.
rationale: The EARAM Delphi validates People, Process, Technology, and Catalyst Enabler as four EA-readiness elements, comprising 14 factors and 45 consensus items across three rounds.

mechanism: Making digital/ICT investment decisions in isolation, without a whole-of-ecosystem adaptive architecture and investment approach, produces redundancies, inefficiencies, inconsistencies, lack of interoperability, and suboptimal use of shared funds; an explicit pipeline connecting strategy to architecture guidance to investment governance to operations (with feedback flowing back upstream) prevents individual actors from making counter-productive isolated decisions.
operationalization_hint: Before approving a digital/ICT investment in a federated or multi-unit organization, verify it has passed through explicit vision/scope, discover (gap analysis against a shared architecture library), and investment-governance stages, with a defined feedback mechanism from operations back to the architecture library.
rationale: The adaptive digital-government model specifies an end-to-end architecture and investment pipeline that connects scope, discovery, implementation, governance, adaptation, and feedback.

raw_condition_label: vertical and horizontal cross-domain alignment as a necessary scope dimension for multi-domain digital transformation
readiness_statement: Beyond aligning within a single functional silo, the organization enables alignment both vertically (across levels of abstraction, e.g., strategy to architecture to solution design) and horizontally (across domains operating at the same level of abstraction, e.g., energy, mobility, and tourism service domains), since digital transformation initiatives increasingly require design and delivery of services driven by integration across domains rather than within isolated silos.
mechanism: Domain-siloed EA practice (e.g., a smart-city energy department architecting independently of mobility or tourism departments) reproduces the fragmentation that digital/ecosystem-oriented transformation is meant to overcome; explicitly designing for both vertical (abstraction-level) and horizontal (domain-level) relationships lets an operating model drive innovation and collaboration across domains.

operationalization_hint: When diagnosing why an EA practice is not delivering alignment benefits, assess each of the five stages (Scoping, Embodiment, Augmentation, Realization, Maintenance) separately rather than treating "EA quality" as a single undifferentiated variable.

mechanism: Different resilience actions are appropriate at different points in a disruption's lifecycle; forecasting/risk-assessment activities (Readiness) address a fundamentally different need than mid-crisis system revision (Responsiveness) or post-crisis sense-making (Recovery), so cataloguing strategies by temporal phase lets an organization identify gaps in its resilience posture across the full disruption lifecycle rather than only preparing for one phase.
operationalization_hint: When assessing EA resilience preparedness, inventory which of the 33 known resilience strategies (per Ramezani & Camarinha-Matos' classification) the organization currently applies in each of the three phases (Readiness/Responsiveness/Recovery), and treat phases with no strategies as priority gaps.

operationalization_hint: When designing a data architecture for a large, multi-domain organization, model three explicit ArchiMate layers -- Domain-Driven Data-as-Product, Self-Serve Data Platform, Federated Governance -- and ensure the governance layer's policies (access, compliance, privacy, exchange, interoperability, documentation) are enforced identically across all domains regardless of each domain's operational autonomy.

rationale: The systematic review identifies a context-dependent spectrum of fine-grained federated, governed, hybrid, value-chain-aligned, and coarse-grained data-mesh archetypes, each with distinct autonomy, complexity, and centralization trade-offs.

readiness_statement: An organization adopting a new architectural/technology paradigm (here, microservices) assesses and advances its readiness along two distinct dimensions in tandem -- technical maturity (API design, service discovery, authentication, performance monitoring, orchestration sophistication) and organizational maturity (talent/hiring, licensing/monetization model, management buy-in, business-model realignment) -- since observed organizations rarely show a high level of maturity on one dimension while remaining low on the other, and full paradigm benefits require both to progress together.
mechanism: Technical implementation of a new architectural style (e.g., building working microservices) is necessarily visible and easy to observe, biasing organizational attention and investment toward the technical dimension; but the paradigm's business value (agility, new revenue models, faster time-to-market) depends equally on organizational changes (talent, licensing, business-model shift) that are less visible and easier to neglect, so tracking only technical maturity produces a false sense of overall transformation readiness.
operationalization_hint: When assessing readiness to adopt a new architectural/technology paradigm, score both a technical-maturity dimension and an organizational-maturity dimension (each on the same level scale) rather than a single combined or technical-only score, and treat a large gap between the two dimensions as a specific risk flag.

mechanism: Across 29 interviews at 4 case firms, interviewees consistently described a causal chain rather than a flat list of independent benefits: artifacts make tacit knowledge explicit ("that is not self-evident," per Delta's CIO), explicit knowledge enables communication ("it's about the conversation and conviction," per Gamma's business owner), and only informed, well-communicated decisions translate into measurable organizational-performance gains -- meaning organizations that document EA artifacts without cultivating the communication/insight cycle around them fail to realize the downstream performance benefit.
operationalization_hint: When justifying investment in EA artifact creation, frame the value case around the causal chain (knowledge conservation -> communication/insight -> decision quality -> organizational performance) rather than listing EA artifacts or values as independent deliverables; prioritize pairing artifact creation with deliberate communication practices (workshops, walkthroughs) rather than "throwing artifacts over the fence."

readiness_statement: The organization designs its Enterprise Information System so that each business process (defined purely by its input and output data) maps directly to one application component and one or more highly-cohesive technology-layer "commands" connected only through data objects (Unix-pipe-style), producing a microservice/loosely-coupled architecture in which business-process analysis and design are simultaneously data-and-application design -- rather than designing business processes, applications, and technology as separate, loosely-synchronized layers.
mechanism: Because each command/component has a single, sophisticated function processing only input/output data, dependencies between components are minimized, letting the organization refactor (re-develop) individual parts of the EIS without cascading changes through the rest of the system; the real-case company achieved measurable multi-year re-development at lower cost specifically because the architecture's loose coupling meant that a single business-process change corresponded to a bounded application-component change rather than a system-wide rewrite.
operationalization_hint: When designing an EIS intended for frequent Agile/Lean-style refactoring, define business processes strictly by their input/output data, map each process 1:1 to an application component built from small, single-function IO-based commands, and connect components only through data objects rather than shared middleware or direct calls.
rationale: The Unicage proposal maps IO-defined business processes to data-linked application components and highly cohesive commands; its case reports lower-cost refactoring, while the paper bounds the method to ERP and calls for further evaluation.

raw_condition_label: EA governance under decentralized/citizen-development technologies (e.g., low-code platforms) requires a deliberately composed portfolio pairing formal instruments with informal enabling practices, not a single centralization/decentralization choice
readiness_statement: The organization governs emerging, decentralization-enabling technologies (such as Low-Code Development Platforms) by deliberately assembling a portfolio of paired strategy clusters -- e.g., formal application registration + informal community "show and tell" sessions; formal risk-tiered guardrails + informal co-design with citizen developers; formal RACI role definitions + informal architect-to-developer mentoring -- rather than choosing either strict centralized top-down control (which citizen developers experience as bureaucratic, eroding the agility that motivated LCDP adoption) or unstructured decentralized enablement (which produces uncontrolled application proliferation, architectural drift, and security exposure).
mechanism: Across three organizations in different regulated sectors (finance, healthcare, manufacturing), purely centralized governance consistently suppressed the innovation/agility benefit that justified adopting decentralized development platforms in the first place, while purely informal/decentralized governance consistently produced shadow-IT-like proliferation, technical debt, and security exposure; pairing formal instruments (which supply clarity, traceability, and safeguards) with informal practices (which cultivate capability, legitimacy, and shared ownership) is what let all three organizations sustain both architectural coherence and development speed simultaneously.
operationalization_hint: When governing any decentralization-enabling technology (low-code platforms, citizen development, or by extension AI-assisted/agentic development), design governance as an explicit portfolio combining at least one formal instrument (registration, risk tiers, RACI) with at least one informal enabling practice (community sessions, co-design, mentoring) for each governance challenge identified, rather than defaulting to either pure top-down control or pure laissez-faire enablement.
page_or_section: Findings section (Strategies; Discussion and conclusion, "A conceptual model of balanced governance")
rationale: The three-case study finds governance effectiveness in deliberately coupling formal instruments with informal enabling practices, rather than selecting a single centralized/decentralized or formal/informal control mode.

raw_condition_label: risk-tiered, proportionate governance (prototype/departmental/enterprise-critical tiers) matches assurance depth to actual business and technical risk rather than applying uniform control
readiness_statement: The organization classifies each decentrally-developed application into a risk tier (e.g., prototype, departmental solution, enterprise-critical application) and scales the depth of governance controls accordingly -- lightweight checklists and automated tests for low-risk prototypes, multi-party security/architecture review for enterprise-critical changes -- with periodic recalibration of tier assignments based on incidents and usage signals, rather than applying either uniformly strict or uniformly lax controls across the entire application portfolio.
mechanism: Applying maximum governance scrutiny to every citizen-developed application (including trivial departmental workflow replacements) creates unnecessary friction that erodes the agility benefit of decentralized development, while applying uniformly light governance to all applications (including those handling sensitive data or supporting critical operations) creates unmanaged risk exposure; explicitly tiering by risk lets the organization preserve speed for the majority of low-stakes applications while concentrating scarce governance attention on the minority that actually warrants it.
operationalization_hint: When governing a growing portfolio of decentrally-developed applications, define at least three risk tiers (e.g., prototype, departmental, enterprise-critical) with explicit, proportionate control requirements per tier, and schedule periodic tier-reassignment reviews triggered by incidents or usage-pattern changes.

readiness_statement: The organization evaluates its EA's dynamism not as a single "flexibility" score but as an aggregated result across four intersecting axes -- five dimensions (Flexibility/Adaptability, Modularity, Expressiveness, Extensibility, Durability/Prediction), a six-step process (Monitor, Compare, Analyze, Plan, Execute, Update Knowledge Base), ArchiMate architectural layers (Business, Application, Technology, Motivation, etc.), and eight metric categories (Structural, Process, Performance, Quality, Alignment, Capacity, Governance, Adoption) -- using the Goal-Question-Metric method to derive concrete, goal-linked metrics for each axis intersection rather than a single composite adaptability rating.
mechanism: Single-score or maturity-stage EA evaluation approaches (e.g., simple maturity models) mask which specific combination of dimension, process-step, layer, and metric-category is actually underperforming; a four-axis GQM structure lets an organization pinpoint, for example, that its Expressiveness dimension specifically lags at the process-alignment metric within the Business layer, producing a targeted rather than generic improvement recommendation.
operationalization_hint: When assessing EA dynamism/adaptability, avoid single composite maturity scores and instead define goals per dimension (flexibility, modularity, expressiveness, extensibility, durability, prediction), derive GQM-style questions and metrics for each dimension across the six-step dynamic-EA process and relevant architecture layers, and aggregate only after granular measurement to preserve diagnostic detail.
rationale: The proposed dynamic-EA evaluation framework uses GQM to organize measurement across dimensions, a six-step process, architectural layers, and metric categories, preserving diagnostic detail beyond a single flexibility score.

readiness_statement: The organization models its business and application architecture layers in a standard notation (ArchiMate) and explicitly establishes two distinct types of inter-layer links between them: implementation links (a business-layer functional concept, e.g., a business process, is implemented by an application-layer functional concept, e.g., an application function) and representation links (a business-layer data concept, e.g., a business object, is represented by an application-layer data concept, e.g., a data object) -- rather than relying on informal, undocumented correspondence between the two layers.
mechanism: Without explicit, typed inter-layer links, software architects lack a structured "cartography" connecting business processes to the application components that realize them, making it impossible to systematically detect alignment problems (e.g., business functions with no corresponding application support, or legacy application functions no longer tied to any current business process); defining implementation (functional) and representation (data) links as first-class, tool-representable relationships (specialized from ArchiMate's Association relationship) creates the structural foundation needed for automated alignment analysis.
operationalization_hint: When establishing Business-IT alignment analysis capability, explicitly model business and application layers in a standard EA notation (ArchiMate or equivalent) and define two link types -- functional implementation links and data representation links -- connecting them, using tool support (e.g., Archi with jArchi scripting) to make the resulting cartography machine-queryable rather than only visually inspectable.

operationalization_hint: When designing or auditing governance for a decentralized, high-autonomy delivery team (not only DevOps, but any team with merged development/operational decision rights), first jointly assess its risk appetite and its process/team maturity, then select a control strategy (ranging from heavier manual preventive approval to fully automated detective-control-based autonomy) matched to that quadrant rather than applying one fixed control regime organization-wide.
rationale: The study reports 17 interviews across nine Dutch companies and identifies risk appetite and DevOps maturity as the two principal factors for a situational control framework. Scope is limited to this DevOps context.

rationale: The MIG model explicitly combines hard governance, soft governance, and contextual aspects because the authors judge all three necessary for maturity assessment. This is an instrument design claim.

rationale: The theory explicitly defines a four-phase standard lifecycle from initiation through shutdown and reports expert agreement that it establishes standardization as an ongoing process.

readiness_statement: Non-compliance with IT standards is fundamentally a goal-misalignment problem: employees follow standards more reliably when adherence (or non-adherence) has visible personal consequences (positive sanctions/rewards for compliance; negative sanctions -- high individual cost -- for deviance), rather than relying on policy documentation alone.
mechanism: Grounded in Organizational Control Theory's Evaluation-Reward construct and management-by-objectives (MBO) literature; confirmed by 6 of 7 experts (one abstained for lack of MBO experience) with Avg 4.33/5 applicability and testable-proposition ratings of 4.00-4.17/5 -- notably lower and more variable than other design principles, with one expert expressing explicit doubt about incentive-based compliance mechanisms.
operationalization_hint: When designing governance for IT (or other) standards in an organization with persistent non-compliance, do not rely solely on documentation and monitoring -- explicitly define and communicate incentives (or costs of non-compliance) tied to individual performance objectives, while recognizing this mechanism has more mixed practitioner buy-in than purely structural/informational mechanisms.
rationale: The theory explicitly proposes incentives and sanctions for IT-standard compliance, while its validation reports lower/more variable acceptance and an expert doubt. It is retained as a qualified design principle.

operationalization_hint: When rolling out a new governance standard or artifact, proactively push concise, benefit-focused communication to all affected users through established channels (not just technical documentation) -- but calibrate volume carefully, since excessive or irrelevant information communicated this way can itself increase user resistance.
rationale: The design theory explicitly specifies proactive information push and its expected cost, manageability, service-quality, and resistance effects. The claims are proposed and expert-reviewed, not causal field effects.

raw_condition_label: environmental turbulence (disruption, crisis) does not directly drive IT organisational resilience -- resilience is not an automatic byproduct of experiencing disruption; instead turbulence acts only indirectly, by increasing organizational investment in IT service quality and IT governance maturity, which are the actual drivers of resilience
readiness_statement: Across 157 surveyed IT leaders, the direct path from environmental turbulence to IT organisational resilience was statistically insignificant (beta=0.034, p>0.05), contradicting the researchers' own a priori expectation -- meaning organizations that merely experience turbulence do not thereby become more resilient; resilience only follows if that turbulence is channeled into strengthening IT service quality (beta=0.156, p<0.05) and IT governance maturity (beta=0.331, p<0.01), which in turn drive resilience.
mechanism: PLS-SEM structural model estimated on cross-sectional survey data from 157 IT leaders/executives across industries, using validated multi-item scales for each construct with reported path coefficients and significance levels.
operationalization_hint: Do not assume that surviving a crisis or disruption automatically builds organizational resilience for the next one -- "reacting" to turbulence is not the resilience mechanism; the mechanism is turbulence prompting deliberate investment in IT governance maturity and IT service quality, which are the actual, measurable resilience-building levers.
rationale: The cross-sectional PLS-SEM study of 157 IT leaders reports a non-significant direct turbulence-resilience path and significant turbulence-to-service-quality/governance paths. Causal language should remain cautious due to the design.

raw_condition_label: an EA organization's placement in the corporate structure (embedded within IT, staff to the CIO, a corporate-level division on par with IT/business, or a corporate staff department reporting to the CEO) determines a monotonic tradeoff between ease of setup and authority over business (not just IT) architecture -- only CEO-level placement enables genuine corporate governance authority, but at the cost of requiring company-wide behavioral and incentive changes
readiness_statement: Four typical EA-organization placements were compared: (1) EA embedded as one team within IT -- simplest to set up, but structurally disconnected from business departments, limited to an IT-centric view of business capabilities, and easily becomes a bottleneck with no authority to compel business-side data or collaboration; (2) EA as a staff department to the CIO -- shifts EA toward strategic IT activities and allows delegating data-collection to IT teams, but remains business-disconnected; (3) EA as a corporate-level division on par with IT and business departments -- improves business relevance and collaboration but has only advisory (not enforcement) power over peer departments; (4) EA as a corporate staff department reporting directly to the CEO -- enables a genuine corporate governance approach with enforcement authority across all departments, but requires enabling/training people company-wide and setting proper incentives, representing the largest organizational change.
mechanism: Comparative framework synthesized from the lead author's first-hand professional experience in EA organizations of types (1)-(3) at a major logistics company, cross-referenced against practitioner literature and the general EAM literature on organizational placement.
operationalization_hint: When advising on where to place a newly-formed (or restructuring) EA function, do not treat organizational placement as a minor implementation detail -- map the intended placement against this four-level hierarchy first, since the authority to compel business-side collaboration and enforce architecture standards (not just produce artifacts) scales directly with how close EA sits to the CEO, and each step up this hierarchy requires a correspondingly larger change-management and incentive-design investment.
rationale: The masterclass compares four EA-placement options and their authority/change tradeoffs, drawing materially on professional experience. It is retained as a practitioner-framework proposition rather than general causal evidence.
